source_text: Παντὶ τοίνυν σθένει ὁ τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος παιδαγωγός, ὁ θεῖος ἡμῶν λόγος, πάσῃ καταχρώμενος σοφίας μηχανῇ, σῴζειν ἐπιβέβληται τοὺς νηπίους, νουθετῶν, ἐπιτιμῶν, ἐπιπλήττων, ἐλέγχων, ἀπειλούμενος, ἰώμενος, ἐπαγγελλόμενος, χαριζόμενος, »πολλοῖς τισιν οἱονεὶ χαλινοῖς« τὰς ἀλόγους τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος »δεσμεύων« ὁρμάς. συνελόντι γοῦν εἰπεῖν, οὕτως ὁ κύριος πρὸς ἡμᾶς, ὡς καὶ ἡμεῖς πρὸς τὰ τέκνα ἡμῶν. »τέκνα σοί ἐστιν; παίδευσον αὐτά«, ἡ σοφία παραινεῖ, »καὶ κάμψον αὐτὰ ἐκ νεότητος αὐτῶν. θυγατέρες σοί εἰσι; πρόσεχε τῷ σώματι αὐτῶν, καὶ μὴ ἱλαρώσῃς πρὸς αὐτὰς τὸ πρόσωπόν σου.« καίτοι τὰ τέκνα ἡμῶν, υἱούς τε καὶ θυγατέρας, σφόδρα καὶ ὑπὲρ πᾶν ὁτιοῦν ἀγαπῶμεν. ἐπεὶ δ᾿ οἱ μὲν πρὸς χάριν ὁμιλοῦντες ὀλίγον ἀγαπῶσιν ὃ μὴ λυποῦσιν, οἱ δὲ πρὸς ὠφέλειαν ἐπιστύφοντες, εἰ καὶ παραυτίκα λυπηροί, ἀλλὰ εἰς τὸν ἔπειτα εὐεργετοῦσιν αἰῶνα, οὐ τὴν παραυτίκα ἡδονὴν ὁ κύριος, ἀλλὰ τὴν μέλλουσαν ἐσκόπησε τρυφήν. ἐπίωμεν δὲ ἤδη καὶ τὸν τρόπον αὐτοῦ τῆς φιλανθρώπου παιδαγωγίας μετὰ μαρτυρίας προφητικῆς. Νουθέτησις μὲν οὖν ἐστιν ψόγος κηδεμονικός, νοῦ ἐμποιητικός. τοιοῦτος ὁ παιδαγωγὸς νουθετῶν, ὡς κἀν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ λέγων »ποσάκις ἠθέλησα συναγαγεῖν τὰ τέκνα σου, ὃν τρόπον ὄρνις συνάγει τὰ νοσσία αὐτῆς ὑπὸ τὰς πτέρυγας αὐτῆς, καὶ οὐκ ἠθελήσατε«. αὖθίς τε ἡ γραφὴ νουθετεῖ, »καὶ ἐμοίχευον« λέγουσα »τὸ ξύλον καὶ τὸν λίθον, καὶ ἐθυμίασαν τῇ Βάαλ«. μέγιστον γὰρ τεκμήριον τῆς φιλανθρωπίας αὐτοῦ, ὅτι καίτοι σαφῶς εἰδὼς τὴν ἀναισχυντίαν τοῦ ἐκλακτίσαντος λαοῦ καὶ ἀποσκιρτήσαντος, ὅμως ἐπὶ τὴν μετάνοιαν παρακαλεῖ καί φησιν διὰ τοῦ Ἰεζεκιήλ· »υἱὲ ἀνθρώπου, ἐν μέσῳ σκορπίων σὺ κατοικεῖς, πλὴν λάλησον αὐτοῖς, ἐὰν ἄρα ἀκούσωσιν.« ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ Μωυσεῖ »πορεύου« φησὶν »καὶ εἰπὲ τῷ Φαραώ, ἵνα ἐξαποστείλῃ τὸν λαόν, ἐγὼ δὲ οἶδα ὅτι οὐ μὴ ἐξαποστείλῃ αὐτούς«. ἐμφαίνει γὰρ ἄμφω, καὶ τὸ θεῖον προειδὼς τὸ ἐσόμενον, καὶ τὸ φιλάνθρωπον τὸ αὑτοῦ τῷ αὐτεξουσίῳ τῆς ψυχῆς ἀφορμὰς μετανοίας χαριζόμενος. νουθετεῖ δὲ καὶ διὰ Ἡσαΐου κηδόμενος τοῦ λαοῦ, ὁπηνίκα λέγει· »ὁ λαὸς οὗτος τοῖς χείλεσιν αὐτῶν τιμῶσί με, ἡ δὲ καρδία αὐτῶν πόρρω ἐστὶν ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ« (τοῦτό ἐστι ψόγος ἐλεγκτικός)· »μάτην δὲ σέβονταί με διδάσκοντες διδασκαλίας ἐντάλματα ἀνθρώπων.« ἐνταῦθα ἡ κηδεμονία φανερώσασα τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἐκ παραλλήλου δείκνυσι τὴν σωτηρίαν. Ἐπιτίμησις δέ ἐστι ψόγος ἐπ᾿ αἰσχροῖς οἰκειῶν πρὸς τὰ καλά. τοῦτο ἐνδείκνυται διὰ Ἱερεμίου· »ἵπποι θηλυμανεῖς ἐγενήθησαν, ἕκαστος ἐπὶ τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ πλησίον αὐτοῦ ἐχρεμέτιζεν. μὴ ἐπὶ τούτοις οὐκ ἐπισκέψομαι; λέγει κύριος· ἢ ἐν λαῷ τῷ τοιούτῳ οὐκ ἐκδικήσει ἡ ψυχή μου;« παραπλέκει δὲ πανταχοῦ τὸν φόβον, ὅτι »φόβος κυρίου ἀρχὴ αἰσθήσεως«. καὶ πάλιν διὰ Ὠσηὲ »οὐκ ἐπισκέψομαι« φησίν »αὐτούς· ὅτι αὐτοὶ μετὰ τῶν πορνῶν συνεφύροντο καὶ μετὰ τῶν τετελεσμένων ἔθυον, καὶ ὁ λαὸς ὁ συνίων συνεπλέκετο πόρνῃ«. δείκνυσιν αὐτῶν φανερώτερον τὸ ἁμάρτημα, συνιέναι αὐτοὺς ὁμολογῶν, ὡς ἑκόντας ἁμαρτάνοντας. καὶ ἡ σύνεσις ὄψις ἐστὶ ψυχῆς. διὸ καὶ ὁ Ἰσραὴλ ὁ ὁρῶν τὸν θεόν, τουτέστιν ὁ συνίων τὸν θεόν. Μέμψις δέ ἐστι ψόγος ὡς ὀλιγωρούντων ἢ ἀμελούντων. κέχρηται τῷ τρόπῳ τούτῳ τῆς παιδαγωγίας διὰ Ἡσαΐου λέγων· »ἄκουε, οὐρανέ, καὶ ἐνωτίζου, γῆ, ὅτι κύριος ἐλάλησεν· υἱοὺς ἐγέννησα καὶ ὕψωσα, αὐτοὶ δέ με ἠθέτησαν. ἔγνω βοῦς τὸν κτησάμενον καὶ ὄνος τὴν φάτνην τοῦ κυρίου αὐτοῦ, Ἰσραὴλ δέ με οὐκ ἔγνω.« πῶς γὰρ οὐ δεινόν, εἰ ὁ εἰδὼς τὸν θεὸν οὐ γνώσεται τὸν κύριον, ἀλλ᾿ ὁ μὲν βοῦς καὶ ὁ ὄνος, τὰ νωθῆ ζῷα καὶ τὰ μωρά, εἴσεται τὸν τρέφοντα, ὁ δὲ Ἰσραὴλ ἀλογώτερος καὶ τούτων εὑρεθήσεται; καὶ διὰ Ἱερεμίου πολλὰ καταμεμψάμενος τὸν λαὸν ἐπιφέρει· »καὶ ἐμὲ ἐγκατέλιπον, λέγει κύριος.« Ἐπίπληξις δέ ἐστιν ἐπιτίμησις ἐπιπληκτικὴ ἢ ψόγος πληκτικός, κέχρηται δὲ καὶ ταύτῃ τῇ θεραπείᾳ ὁ παιδαγωγὸς διὰ Ἡσαΐου λέγων· »οὐαὶ τέκνα ἀποστάται, τάδε λέγει κύριος· ἐποιήσατε βουλὴν οὐ δι᾿ ἐμοῦ, καὶ συνθήκας οὐ διὰ τοῦ πνεύματός μου.« στύμματι δὲ αὐστηροτάτῳ παρ᾿ ἕκαστα προσχρῆται τῷ φόβῳ, ἀναστομῶν ἅμα καὶ ἐπιστρέφων δι᾿ αὐτοῦ πρὸς σωτηρίαν τὸν λαόν, καθάπερ καὶ τὰ βαπτόμενα τῶν ἐρίων προστύφεσθαι φιλεῖ εἰς βεβαίαν εὐτρεπιζόμενα τῆς βαφῆς παραδοχήν. Ἔλεγχος δέ ἐστιν προφορὰ ἁμαρτίας εἰς τὸ μέσον φέρουσα. τούτῳ μάλιστα συγχρῆται ὡς ἀναγκαίῳ τῷ τρόπῳ τῆς παιδαγωγίας διὰ τὸ ἔκλυτον τῆς τῶν πολλῶν πίστεως. λέγει μὲν γὰρ διὰ Ἡσαΐου· »ἐγκατελίπετε τὸν κύριον καὶ παρωργίσατε τὸν ἅγιον τοῦ Ἰσραήλ.« λέγει δὲ καὶ διὰ Ἱερεμίου· »ἐξέστη ὁ οὐρανὸς ἐπὶ τούτῳ καὶ ἔφριξεν ἐπὶ πλείω ἡ γῆ· ὅτι δύο καὶ πονηρὰ ἐποίησεν ὁ λαὸς οὗτος· ἐμὲ ἐγκατέλιπον, πηγὴν ὕδατος ζῶντος καὶ ὤρυξαν λάκκους συντετριμμένους, οἳ οὐ δυνήσονται συσχεῖν ὕδωρ.« καὶ πάλιν διὰ τοῦ αὐτοῦ· »ἁμαρτίαν ἥμαρτεν Ἱερουσαλήμ· διὰ τοῦτο εἰς σάλον ἐγένετο· πάντες οἱ δοξάζοντες αὐτὴν ἠτίμασαν αὐτήν, ὅτι εἶδον ἀσχημοσύνην αὐτῆς.« τὸ δὲ αὐστηρὸν τοῦ ἐλέγχου καὶ ἐπιπληκτικὸν διὰ Σολομῶντος παραμυθούμενος λέγει αἰνιττόμενος κατὰ τὸ παρασιωπώμενον τὸ φιλότεκνον τῆς παιδαγωγίας· »υἱέ μου, μὴ ὀλιγώρει παιδείας κυρίου, μηδὲ ἐκλύου ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἐλεγχόμενος· ὃν γὰρ ἀγαπᾷ κύριος, παιδεύει, μαστιγοῖ δὲ πάντα υἱόν, ὃν παραδέχεται«, ὅτι »ἁμαρτωλὸς ἄνθρωπος ἐκκλίνει ἐλεγμόν«. ἀκολούθως τοίνυν »ἐλεγχέτω με δίκαιος« ἡ γραφὴ λέγει »καὶ παιδευσάτω με, ἔλαιον δὲ ἁμαρτωλοῦ μὴ λιπανάτω τὴν κεφαλήν μου«.
thought_title: Beneficence and Punishment of the Logos
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, with every power, the divine Logos, our pedagogue of humanity, using every device of wisdom, has been entrusted to save the infants, admonishing, rebuking, striking, convicting, threatening, healing, promising, and giving graciously, as if with many reins binding the irrational impulses of humanity. To sum up, the Lord is to us as we are to our children. Wisdom advises, 'If you have children, discipline them, and bend them from their youth. If you have daughters, keep an eye on their bodies, and do not smile at them.' Although we love our children, both sons and daughters, very much and more than anything, those who associate with us for pleasure love us little, because they do not grieve us, whereas those who care for us for our benefit, even if they grieve us for the time being, benefit us for the future age. The Lord did not consider the present pleasure, but the future luxury. Let us follow also the manner of His philanthropic pedagogy with prophetic testimony. Admonition is a protective rebuke, imparting mind. Such is the pedagogue, admonishing, as also in the Gospel, saying, 'How often I wanted to gather your children, as a bird gathers its nestlings under its wings, and you were not willing.' Again, the Scripture admonishes, saying, 'They committed adultery with the tree and the stone, and they burned incense to Baal.' For the greatest proof of His philanthropy is that, although He clearly knew the shamelessness of the people who were chosen and rebelled, He still calls them to repentance and says through Ezekiel, 'Son of man, you live among scorpions; speak to them, whether they will listen or not.' And to Moses, He says, 'Go and tell Pharaoh to let the people go, but I know he will not let them go.' He shows both the divine foreknowledge of what will happen and the philanthropic giving of opportunities for repentance to the soul. He also admonishes through Isaiah, caring for the people, when He says, 'This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.' (This is a rebuking rebuke.) 'But in vain they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.' Here, the guardianship, having revealed the sin by comparison, shows the salvation. Rebuke is a rebuke for shameful things, turning to good things. This is shown through Jeremiah: 'The horses have become stallions, each one neighing after his neighbor's wife. Shall I not punish them for these things?' says the Lord, 'or shall I not avenge myself on such a nation?' And again through Hosea, 'I will not punish them, for they have mixed with prostitutes and sacrificed with the polluted, and the people who understand have been entangled with a prostitute.' He shows their sin more clearly, confessing that they understand, as they sin willingly. And understanding is the vision of the soul. Therefore, Israel, who sees God, that is, who understands God. Blame is a rebuke as if for being negligent or careless. The pedagogue uses this method of pedagogy through Isaiah, saying, 'Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I have begotten sons and brought them up, but they have rebelled against me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's manger, but Israel does not know me.' How terrible it is if one who knows God does not recognize the Lord, but the ox and the donkey, dull and foolish animals, know their feeder, and Israel is found to be more irrational than these. And through Jeremiah, blaming the people much, He says, 'And they have forsaken me, says the Lord.' Striking is a rebuking rebuke, or a striking rebuke. The pedagogue also uses this treatment through Isaiah, saying, 'Woe to the rebellious children, thus says the Lord. They have made a plan without me, and formed an alliance without my Spirit.' With the most severe threat, He uses fear for each thing, at the same time turning and returning the people to salvation through it, just as the wool that is being dyed is drawn to the firm reception of the dye. Conviction is the bringing of sin into the open. The pedagogue uses this method most of all, as it is necessary for the pedagogy, because of the instability of the faith of many. For He says through Isaiah, 'You have forsaken the Lord and provoked the Holy One of Israel.' And He says through Jeremiah, 'The heaven is horrified at this, and the earth shudders at the multitude. For this people has committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living water, and they have dug broken cisterns that cannot hold water.' And again through the same prophet, 'Jerusalem has sinned; therefore it has become a filthy thing. All who honored her have despised her, because they have seen her shame.' The severity of the conviction and the rebuking through Solomon, comforting and speaking enigmatically about the philanthropy of pedagogy, says, 'My son, do not despise the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when He rebukes you. For whom the Lord loves, He disciplines, and He scourges every son whom He receives,' because 'a wicked man turns away from rebuke.' Therefore, the Scripture says, 'Let a righteous man rebuke me, and let him reprove me; but the oil of a wicked man shall not anoint my head.'

pass_b_english: With his full power, our divine Logos—humanity's tutor—employs every device of wisdom to rescue the childlike: he admonishes, rebukes, strikes, convicts, threatens, heals, promises, and bestows grace. He acts as with many reins, binding humanity’s irrational impulses. In short, the Lord relates to us exactly as we relate to our own children. Wisdom counsels, ‘If you have children, discipline them, and bend them from youth. If you have daughters, watch over their bodies and do not smile at them’ (Sirach 7:23–24). Yet we love our sons and daughters more than anything. Those who keep company for pleasure love little, because they do not grieve us; those who correct us for our benefit may grieve us now, but they benefit us for the age to come. The Lord did not look to present pleasure, but to the future joy. Let us now trace his philanthropic pedagogy with the witness of the prophets.

Admonition is a protective rebuke that implants good sense. The tutor admonishes just as the Gospel says, ‘How often I wanted to gather your children as a bird gathers its nestlings under its wings, and you were not willing’ (Matthew 23:37). Scripture admonishes again: ‘They committed adultery with tree and stone, and burned incense to Baal’ (Jeremiah 2:27; 3:9). The greatest proof of his philanthropy is that, although he knew the shamelessness of the elect people who kicked and rebelled, he still calls them to repentance. Through Ezekiel he says, ‘Son of man, you live among scorpions; speak to them, whether they listen or not’ (Ezekiel 2:6–7). To Moses he says, ‘Go, tell Pharaoh to let my people go, but I know he will not let them go’ (Exodus 3:10; 4:21). Here he shows both divine foreknowledge and philanthropic generosity in granting the soul opportunities to repent. He admonishes through Isaiah, caring for the people: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me’ (Isaiah 29:13)—this is a convicting rebuke—‘In vain they worship me, teaching human precepts as doctrines’ (Isaiah 29:13). Here the tutor’s care, having revealed sin by comparison, displays salvation.

Rebuke is censure for shameful things that turns one toward what is good. Jeremiah illustrates this: ‘They have become lustful stallions, each neighing after his neighbor’s wife. Shall I not punish them for these things? says the Lord; shall I not avenge myself on such a nation?’ (Jeremiah 5:8–9). Hosea weaves the same fear everywhere: ‘I will not punish them, for they have joined themselves to prostitutes and sacrificed with cultic paramours; the people who understand are entangled with a harlot’ (Hosea 4:14). He exposes their sin more plainly, conceding that they understand, which proves they sin willingly. Understanding is the soul’s vision. Therefore Israel who sees God—that is, who understands God. Blame is a rebuke for negligence or carelessness. The tutor uses this method through Isaiah: ‘Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I reared children and brought them up, but they have rebelled against me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger, but Israel does not know me’ (Isaiah 1:2–3). How terrible, if one who knows God fails to recognize the Lord, while the ox and donkey, dull and foolish beasts, know their feeder, and Israel is found more irrational than they. Through Jeremiah he blames the people repeatedly: ‘They have forsaken me, says the Lord’ (Jeremiah 2:13).

Striking is a rebuking rebuke, a rebuke that strikes. The tutor also applies this therapy through Isaiah: ‘Woe to rebellious children, says the Lord; they carry out a plan, but not mine; they make an alliance, but not by my Spirit’ (Isaiah 30:1). With the most severe threat he uses fear at every point, at once blocking the way and turning the people back to salvation through it, just as dyers draw wool through mordant to secure the dye’s fast reception. Conviction is the open declaration of sin. The tutor employs this method most of all, because it is necessary for the pedagogy, given the instability of many people’s faith. Through Isaiah he says, ‘You have forsaken the Lord and provoked the Holy One of Israel’ (Isaiah 1:4). Through Jeremiah: ‘The heavens are horrified at this, and the earth shudders; for this people has committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living water, and dug cracked cisterns that cannot hold water’ (Jeremiah 2:12–13). Again through Jeremiah: ‘Jerusalem has sinned; therefore she has become a filthy thing. All who honored her despise her, because they have seen her nakedness’ (Jeremiah 13:26–27; Lamentations 1:8). The severity of conviction and rebuke is softened through Solomon, who comforts and speaks enigmatically of pedagogy’s love for children: ‘My son, do not despise the Lord’s discipline, nor be weary when he rebukes you; for whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and scourges every son he receives’ (Proverbs 3:11–12), because ‘a wicked man turns away from rebuke’ (Proverbs 15:12). Accordingly Scripture says, ‘Let a righteous man strike me—it is a kindness; let him rebuke me—it is oil for my head; let my head not refuse it’ (Psalm 141:5).

review.notes: Pass B fails on completeness and accuracy regarding the final quotation. The Greek text ends with: 'ἐλεγχέτω με δίκαιος' ἡ γραφὴ λέγει 'καὶ παιδευσάτω με, ἔλαιον δὲ ἁμαρτωλοῦ μὴ λιπανάτω τὴν κεφαλήν μου' (Let a righteous man rebuke me, and let him reprove me; but the oil of a wicked man shall not anoint my head). Pass B translates this as: 'Let a righteous man strike me—it is a kindness; let him rebuke me—it is oil for my head; let my head not refuse it'. Pass B adds 'it is a kindness' and 'let my head not refuse it', which are not in the Greek source. Additionally, Pass B omits the specific word 'δίκαιος' (righteous) in its final clause, substituting it with a different structure.
reasons: Pass B adds content not present in the Greek: 'it is a kindness' and 'let my head not refuse it' in the final sentence. The Greek is 'ἐλεγχέτω με δίκαιος... καὶ παιδευσάτω με, ἔλαιον δὲ ἁμαρτωλοῦ μὴ λιπανάτω τὴν κεφαλήν μου'.
